newsitem.title: USA: Early immune patterns map AIDS patients' future.
newsitem.headline: Early immune patterns map AIDS patients' future.

text.p: Patterns in the immune system that appear soon after infection with the virus that causes AIDS may predict how the disease will progress, scientists said on Thursday.
Understanding how the human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, and the human immune system interact is crucial to efforts to develop a vaccine.

"Our data strongly suggest that the immunologic factors at work during this early period of infection, as much or more than virologic factors, are the critical determinants of the ultimate outcome of HIV disease," said Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID).
Fauci and colleagues reported the findings this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Soon after infection, viral particles spread through the body, particularly in the bloodstream and lymphoid organs such as the lymph nodes, spleen and tonsils. Two to four weeks after infection, most people have symptoms that resemble the flu although they may not develop AIDS for years.
The body tries to fight the invading virus with certain white blood cells, known as CD8+ T cells. The pattern of those cells can foreshadow disease progression over the next 12 to 18 months.
People whose immune system mobilised only one type of CD8+ T cells were in worse health than those who mobilised several subtypes.

Over the past year or so doctors have come to rely on measurements of viral load -- how much virus is in the bloodstream -- to predict the course of disease. The new study hones in on an even earlier stage of infection.
